How touching, by comparison, is the cry:
To these back-to-idealism people I can answer only with the words of Castruccio Castracani:
Now that you are coming out, you have no reason to be ashamed.
You should have been ashamed when you went in.
“Are We at a Turning Point in World History?” That is the question Shotwell used as the title of his Berlin lecture of March 1927.
Otherwise the question itself could not have been asked.
So there is a turning point: from the static to the dynamic, from repetition to change, from dependence on nature to freedom.
The most important thing, however, is our awareness of the turning point. That awareness shows that we are facing a choice: continue further along the path of dynamism, or stop, reflect, and return?
To continue means continuing toward the total rule of the dynamic. We have now reached the point at which this dynamic world must completely destroy the old one.
The free creative power of man must take complete possession of nature.

Complete possession means possession not only of the world outside man but also of man’s own physical and psychological nature. That is the problem of totality. It creates the compulsion toward total planning. It creates this total human power. It removes every remaining natural limit.
The problem is now becoming conscious.
And the despair of the Germans showed itself in the fact that, in the name of the old and the natural, they stumbled headlong into the most shameless dynamism of the new.
Again and again: this is the problem of totality. And it arises from our awareness that we have reached this turning point.
That is what the dynamic creators of their own world must now say.
Or rather: that is what they must now do, even if they would prefer not to speak openly about it in front of these blood-soaked enfants terribles.
5 September 1947, journey to Dortmund (6 September to Menden)
So Annette—or perhaps here it is better to say the Droste—and Heinrich von Kleist: that would have been one of those meetings that German circumstances never permit.
In Dortmund, an especially friendly and intelligent kind of foolish and wise virgin. I am delighted by this friendliness in the middle of this shattered great city.
You probably saw nothing of that, Georges Bernanos, when you were so horrified by the destroyed German cities and apparently thought cities like these must be the end of the world.
Geneva and the audience you have today would seem much more terrifying to me.
Above all, your own situation would frighten me.

Unless you yourself know that you are in the position of Kierkegaard’s clown: the clown who cries “Fire!” because the building really is burning, while the audience applauds because it thinks the cry is an excellent joke. But that is probably the situation of every intellectual, every clerc.
Perhaps it is even the definition of the intellectual: the person who knows and speaks instead of remaining silent. Or who writes instead of remaining silent.
Speaking in written form is the worst of all. That black trail of ink that Annette feared so much, with death and life following “softly, creeping” behind it.
“That passes clearly east and west as a sign.”)
Paul Adams knew the passage from Le Mendiant ingrat of 22 June 1894:
“I tell you this on behalf of God.”
Fumet leaves it out. So does the new edition of 1928.
Am I right to hide away here in this comfortable form of home?
Reading my notes from 1912–14 leaves me astonished by the infinite immobility of events, by the immobility of what people call time. Or, which amounts to the same thing: the infinite patience of God.
Nothing of what people call development.
Nothing essential in the way of education.
Again and again I am frightened by the hostility that the mere speaking of the word and name “enemy” has unleashed against me.
Did I violate some secret agreement?
Perhaps even one of the hidden mysteries of this age?
Or did I merely violate one of those harmless lies people need in order to live?
One of those secret agreements that even the simplest age cannot survive without—agreements that are literally necessary for life?
After all, even a gang of criminals cannot function without them.
Did I violate some raison d’être or raison d’état?
In today’s Epistle, on the fifteenth Sunday after Pentecost, I hear:
Your enemies are my enemies, and those who strike you I will strike.
And in Claudel, in his introduction to Tardif de Moidrey, I read:
“And raison d’état, if you please! Everyone, every single person, has a raison d’état of his own.” That applies even to our sensitivity toward particular words and concepts.
In the house of a hanged man, one does not speak of the rope?
Or: among the proscribed, one does not speak of the list?
Or: in Hell, one must not paint the Devil on the wall?
Had the enemy already been banished into theology?
Does he return in mythology, which arrives with mass society and belongs to it?

So: you are on earth in order to know God. But Marx says: the point is not to know but to change. That means: to master and make useful. So now you are on earth in order to change God, master God, and make God useful to you.
No one was horrified by that.

But people were horrified by the observation that there is a distinction between friend and enemy, and that something called enmity still exists among human beings. That was a crude grab at the sensitive spot.
The Devil jumped up when someone beat the bushes in that particular place and taught the naive bush-beater a lesson.
Claudel, in his introduction to Abbé Tardif de Moidrey’s commentary on Ruth, 1937:

“The Antichrist, the black Christ, the negative shadow of Christ, began his career together with the other. Every ray that increases the splendor of the one adds another refusal and another outline to the blasphemy of the other … The Christian always has to force a path for himself, crucifix in hand, through the coils and jaws of the two beasts: the beast of the land, which is temporal, and the beast of the sea, which is spiritual.”
Heart of Jesus, filled with reproach.
Beethoven, then, is the French Revolution. But not only Robespierre. He is also Rousseau.

The Pastoral Symphony belongs to it too. Only that makes Beethoven so astonishingly complete. It is the first and only “landscape” in the sense of a secularized paradise. It still believes completely in landscape. This Rousseau-like effect in the Pastoral is even more important than Rousseau’s influence on Kant, Fichte, the young Hegel, Hölderlin, and Schiller.
Again I am astonished by how closely my thinking is related to Hauriou’s.
Whoever says ceremony or formality is speaking of an action performed in one continuous stretch of time—and, I would add, in one particular place.
A ceremony belongs essentially to the present.

Once it has ended, it is difficult to imagine later additions being attached to it. That is the problem of the irrevocability of an act of state. This is also the unity of place, time, and action, especially in the jurist Corneille.
Or Hauriou: territory helps provide us with the idea of what is public.
Or: law is a general provision.
Or his remarks on the imperative character of law.
And so on, and so on.
In this man I recognize my elder brother. What happiness there is in meetings and recognitions of this kind.
How can legality survive as a system once nobody can any longer believe in the rationality of the législateur, the lawgiver?

Once nobody can even believe in his honest intention to remain impartial? We must recognize the connection between legality, rationality, and political neutrality between parties. It is already there in Bodin, Republic, p. 636, and elsewhere.
From Cardinal Passionei’s opinion of 1753, written for Benedict XIV on the question of the canonization of Cardinal Robert Bellarmine.
The issue concerns Bellarmine’s autobiography “from faith,” which he wrote in 1613, at the age of seventy-one, at the request of a friend.
